Osmosis & Diffusion 3D Lab

Lettuce goes crisp in water. Salted cucumber slices go limp. Seawater makes you thirstier. All three come down to how water and other molecules cross a cell membrane. Weigh potato cores to track water moving by osmosis, use agar cubes to find out why cells have to be small, then zoom in to watch single molecules cross a membrane four different ways. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

💧 Osmosis

water moves toward the side with MORE solute

Water crosses the membrane, but most dissolved particles cannot. Hypotonic solution: water enters the cell. Hypertonic: water leaves. Isotonic: no net change.

📦 The big idea

passive = down the gradient · active = needs ATP

Diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion need no energy from the cell. Active transport pumps particles “uphill” and costs ATP.

Teacher notes

Three self-contained labs in one offline HTML file for grades 9–12 biology. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks and iPads included). Nothing is uploaded; results are saved in the browser on that device only, and students can download their data as a CSV file.

Learning goals

Students will be able to:

  • Carry out a controlled investigation of osmosis in plant tissue and calculate percent change in mass.
  • Draw a line of best fit and use it to estimate the isotonic point of a tissue.
  • Calculate surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio, and use them to explain why cells are small.
  • Use a particle model to compare osmosis, simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport.
  • Predict what happens to animal and plant cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions.

Suggested sequence (3 class periods)

  • Lab 1 · Potato Osmosis (1 period): The potato core investigation. Six sucrose concentrations (0.0–1.0 M), start and end mass, percent change in mass, three trials, graph with line of best fit, isotonic point. Extensions: compare tissues; compare soaking times.
  • Lab 2 · Why Cells Are Small (1 period): The agar cube diffusion lab. Surface area, volume and SA : V for 1, 2 and 3 cm cubes; depth of diffusion; percent of volume reached.
  • Lab 3 · Inside the Membrane (1 period): Particle models of osmosis, simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport; tonicity and its effect on red blood cells and plant cells; comparison table.

What the models assume

  • Lab 1: the isotonic points are set at about 0.28 M (potato), 0.40 M (carrot) and 0.50 M (sweet potato). Real values vary with variety, age and storage; published class results for potato are usually 0.2–0.35 M. Each mass has a small random error, like a real balance.
  • Lab 2: the acid front moves in 0.4 cm in 10 minutes and slows with time (distance ∝ √time). In the hands-on version the cubes are agar made with an indicator and a little base; vinegar turns the pink indicator colorless.
  • Lab 3 is a particle cartoon: not to scale, hugely slowed, and with far fewer molecules than a real cell. Net water movement emerges because water molecules held around solute particles cannot enter the channels. In real membranes water also crosses the lipid layer slowly; here it crosses only through aquaporins.

Misconceptions these labs target

  • “In osmosis the sugar moves.” In Labs 1 and 3 only water crosses; the solute stays put.
  • “Molecules stop moving at equilibrium.” In Lab 3 particles keep crossing in both directions when the numbers are equal.
  • “A bigger cell has less surface area.” Lab 2: the 3 cm cube has the most surface area but the least per cm³.
  • ““Hypertonic” describes the cell.” Tonicity is always stated for the solution compared with the cell.
  • “Plant cells burst in pure water.” The cell wall pushes back; the plant cell becomes turgid, while the red blood cell bursts.
  • “Active transport just means fast transport.” Only the pump moves particles from low to high concentration, and it stops without ATP.

Standards

  • NGSS: Supports HS-LS1-3, HS-LS1-2. NGSS has no performance expectation that names osmosis or membrane transport. These labs build the disciplinary core idea LS1.A (structure and function) and the evidence base for HS-LS1-3: cells keep their internal conditions stable by controlling what crosses the membrane. Practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Developing and Using Models. Crosscutting concepts: Structure and Function; Stability and Change; Scale, Proportion, and Quantity.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42, adopted 2021): B.5C (investigate homeostasis through the cellular transport of molecules). Scientific and engineering practices: B.1B, B.1E, B.1F, B.1G, B.2B, B.2C.
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments and taking measurements); RST.9-10.7 (translate information between words, tables, graphs and equations); HSN-Q.A.1 (use units to understand problems and guide multistep solutions; choose and interpret scales in graphs); HSS-ID.B.6 (represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot and describe how they are related); HSG-MG.A.1 (use geometric shapes, their measures and their properties to describe objects).
  • AP Biology (2025 course framework): 2.2 Cell Size; 2.4 Membrane Permeability; 2.5 Membrane Transport; 2.6 Facilitated Diffusion; 2.7 Tonicity and Osmoregulation.

Safety and risk assessment

Using the simulation (screen only: no chemicals or equipment)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Screen useEye strain, poor postureEach lab fits one class period. Build in a short break; look away from the screen every 20 minutes.
Flashing or moving imagesPhotosensitivity, motion discomfortNo flashing or strobing content. The 3D camera moves only when the student moves it; fly-through moves become instant jumps when the device is set to reduce motion.
Student dataPrivacyRuns offline. No accounts, no tracking and nothing uploaded. Results stay in the browser on that device and can be cleared at any time.

Potato cores and agar cubes (optional hands-on versions of Labs 1 and 2)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Cork borer and knifeCuts and puncture woundsCut down onto a board, away from fingers; push the core out with a rod, never a finger.
Sucrose solutionsSticky, slippery spillsWipe up spills right away.
Food materials in the labEating contaminated foodNo eating or drinking, even though the materials are food.
Sodium hydroxide used to make the agarCorrosive to eyes and skinTeacher prepares the cubes in advance, with goggles and gloves.
Phenolphthalein indicatorHealth hazard (suspected carcinogen); the alcohol solution is flammableTeacher only. Many districts restrict it: agar made with bromothymol blue (blue → yellow in vinegar) is a common substitute.
Vinegar (dilute acetic acid)Eye irritationSplash goggles; rinse splashes with water.
Used cubes and coresBlocked drainsDispose of in the trash, not the sink.

This table supports, but does not replace, your own school or district risk assessment. Follow your chemical hygiene plan, read the SDS for every chemical, and check state and district rules before any hands-on activity.

Accessibility

  • Results are shown in tables as well as graphs.
  • Water, solute and ions differ in size and label as well as color.
  • All controls work with the keyboard: Tab to move, Enter or Space to press, arrow keys on sliders. In the 3D view, arrow keys rotate and the + and − keys zoom.
  • Gray controls cannot be used yet. They stay reachable and explain why when pressed.
  • Nothing is shown by color alone: right and wrong answers are marked ✓ and ✗, and results are given in words and numbers.
  • No sound, no flashing content, and no time limits that cannot be repeated. Text stays readable when the browser is zoomed to 200%.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan.
